svg.title: A mother reports her newborn had bloody mucus in the stool earlier and is worried. Which nursing interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
svg.desc: Look first, then report. Blood in a newborn’s stool is reported promptly — the day you see it, not after waiting to see if it clears. It is often swallowed maternal blood from the birth or a cracked nipple, but only the provider’s workup can say so. So see the stool first — colour, amount and consistency — note how she looks and feeds, then document and notify . Then give her the map: meconium (thick, tarry, dark green-black) for the first day or two, transitional (greenish-brown, looser) around days 3 to 4, then milk stools — seedy and mustard-yellow if breastfed, paler and firmer if formula-fed — and ask her to report any further blood straight away. “That's normal” or “it should settle by day 3” is a reassurance nobody can give before the workup , and it dismisses her. Nothing here warrants NPO.
